practice1.prompt: fix the comparison so a score on the pass mark counts as a pass

cases.name: three of the four scores pass

hiddenCases.name: a score exactly on the mark passes
works for any scores and any pass mark
hiddenCases.reference:
def count_passing(scores, pass_mark):
    return len([s for s in scores if s >= pass_mark])

practice1.hint: Nothing crashes, so the only evidence is the gap between 3 and 1. Two of the four scores are exactly 6. Ask which comparison lets a score equal to the pass mark through.

questions.prompt: What makes a logical error harder to find than a runtime error?
choices: The program runs cleanly and gives a wrong answer, so nothing points at the line
It only appears in large programs
questions.explain: A runtime error names a line for you. A logical error produces an answer, and the only clue is that the answer is not the one you expected.

questions.prompt: To count scores that reach the pass mark, the comparison must be ___ rather than a plain greater-than.
questions.explain: A score exactly on the mark is a pass. Plain greater-than silently excludes everyone sitting on the boundary, which is where off-by-one bugs live.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson insist you work out the expected answer before running the code?
choices: Without a known right answer you cannot tell a wrong output from a correct one
Python needs it to run the function
questions.explain: The bug here is only visible because 3 was expected and 1 arrived. Run it without knowing, and 1 looks like an answer.

questions.prompt: Which of these are classic off-by-one mistakes?
choices: Stopping a range one item early
Starting a count at 1 when the list is indexed from 0
questions.explain: All three are a boundary being crossed one step too early or too late. A bad name makes code harder to read but does not change what it computes.
